Family Health

Trachelectomy: removing the cervix and preserving pregnancy options

Updated: October 11, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

The cervix connects the womb to the vagina. Trachelectomy removes cervical tissue while retaining the womb, sometimes as treatment for a carefully selected early cervical cancer. It may preserve the possibility of carrying a pregnancy, but neither pregnancy nor freedom from recurrence is guaranteed. Decisions belong with a specialist gynaecological cancer team and should include your fertility wishes.

What simple and radical trachelectomy mean

A simple trachelectomy removes the cervix without the same surrounding-tissue removal as a radical operation. Radical trachelectomy also removes tissue beside the cervix and part of the upper vagina. Lymph-node assessment may be needed separately. The extent depends on the cancer findings; removing the cervix does not always mean radical surgery.

The womb and usually the ovaries are retained. Hysterectomy removes the womb and prevents carrying a pregnancy; a cone biopsy removes a smaller piece of cervical tissue. These procedures have different indications and risks. Ask exactly what is proposed, what will remain and what findings could change the plan.

Why it may be offered, and what HPV means

The main reason discussed here is selected early cervical cancer. Persistent high-risk human papillomavirus, HPV, causes most cervical cancers. HPV is common and usually clears; CDC estimates about nine in ten infections clear within two years. A positive HPV test alone is not cancer and is not an indication to remove the cervix. Abnormal cells need their own recommended follow-up.

Cervical screening depends on having a cervix, age, previous results and risk, including immune suppression, rather than assumptions about gender or partners. Smoking increases risk. Discuss HPV vaccination and local screening guidance. Early cancer may cause no symptoms; unusual vaginal bleeding, pelvic pain or pain during sex needs assessment even after a reassuring screening result.

Who may be suitable for fertility-sparing treatment

A specialist team reviews the biopsy, cancer type, stage, size, depth of invasion, imaging, lymph nodes and ability to obtain clear margins. Many standard candidates have a small cancer confined to the cervix, usually under or around 2 cm depending on the guideline and other findings. Size alone never establishes eligibility; some aggressive cancer types are unsuitable.

Some very early, low-risk cancers can be treated with a cone biopsy or simple trachelectomy rather than a radical procedure. Others require more extensive surgery or chemoradiotherapy. Larger tumours are not routinely treated with fertility-sparing surgery. Ask about cancer control and pregnancy risks together, including the possibility of abandoning the fertility-sparing plan if nodes or margins are involved.

Benefits and limits compared with hysterectomy

Keeping the womb can preserve a route to pregnancy that hysterectomy cannot. Suitable patients can have effective cancer treatment, but comparisons between procedures depend on careful selection and follow-up. Broad comparisons of survival between procedures and published pregnancy percentages are not reliable personal predictions. Discuss outcomes for your particular cancer and proposed operation.

A shorter admission or less blood loss in a small study does not make one operation universally better. Vaginal, open abdominal, laparoscopic and surgeon-controlled robotic approaches have different trade-offs. Smaller incisions do not automatically mean safer cancer outcomes; evidence from radical hysterectomy must not be presented as a direct trachelectomy result. Ask why the recommended route fits your situation.

Preparation and what happens during surgery

Before surgery, expect assessment of anaesthetic fitness, medicines, allergies and previous operations, plus imaging and pathology review as needed. Discuss fertility preservation before treatment begins and consent for possible changes. Follow your hospital's eating, drinking and medicine instructions. The operation is generally performed under general anaesthesia, with intravenous access and a urinary catheter.

When indicated, the surgeon assesses pelvic lymph nodes and removes the planned cervical and surrounding tissue. The womb is joined to the remaining vaginal tissue, usually with a permanent supporting stitch, or cerclage, and an opening for menstrual blood. Removed tissue is examined. Involved nodes or margins may require a different treatment plan, including chemoradiotherapy or further surgery; this is not one automatic sequence for everyone.

Risks and possible longer-term effects

Risks include bleeding, infection, blood clots, anaesthetic complications and injury to the bladder, ureters, bowel or blood vessels. Temporary or persistent difficulty emptying the bladder, urine leakage, constipation, adhesions and altered sensation in the upper thighs can occur. Tell the team about continuing symptoms; do not assume they are inevitable or untreatable.

Pelvic lymph-node treatment can lead to lymphocysts or lymphoedema, commonly involving the legs, lower abdomen or genital area, rather than a universal pattern of arm swelling. Periods may change or become painful; narrowing of the remaining opening can obstruct menstrual flow. Seek review for new swelling, absent periods with pain, persistent discharge or urinary problems.

Hospital stay, catheter care and recovery

Admission and recovery vary with the operation, complications, health and support at home. Some services describe a few nights in hospital; recovery usually takes several weeks and can take longer. A catheter may remain after discharge until the bladder empties safely. Learn its care and the removal or review plan; do not remove it yourself or accept a fixed one- or two-week timetable as universal.

Use prescribed pain relief and constipation treatment, and follow wound-care and clot-prevention instructions. Increase gentle walking gradually while allowing rest. Obtain individual clearance for lifting, exercise, stairs, driving and work; driving also requires safe movement and freedom from impairing medicines. Avoid vaginal penetration, tampons and swimming until the team says healing is sufficient; around six weeks is a common instruction, not a guarantee.

Sexual health and emotional recovery

Pain, altered desire, tiredness, body-image concerns and anxiety can affect intimacy. You do not have to resume penetrative sex on a deadline. After healing and clinical clearance, return at your pace and seek help for pain, bleeding or persistent difficulties. Lubrication, pelvic-health care or psychosexual support may be appropriate after assessment.

A small older study does not mean everyone develops sexual problems or that desire always returns at twelve months. Cancer and uncertainty about fertility can be distressing even when treatment succeeds. Ask the specialist nurse about counselling, partner support if wanted, and practical help during recovery.

Pregnancy after trachelectomy

Pregnancy can be possible, but scarring or a narrowed opening may make conception harder, and some people need fertility treatment. Arrange preconception advice and ask when trying is medically appropriate. Use contraception until the cancer team clears you; local waiting recommendations differ. There is no universal pregnancy-success percentage or promise that preserving the womb preserves fertility fully.

Pregnancy after fertility-sparing cervical surgery needs specialist high-risk care because miscarriage, early waters breaking and premature birth are more likely. A permanent cerclage does not remove those risks. Delivery after simple or radical trachelectomy with a permanent cerclage is by caesarean section; timing and monitoring are individual. Contact the maternity team promptly with pregnancy, and urgently for bleeding, fluid loss or contractions.

Warning signs after surgery

Contact the surgical team urgently for fever or chills, increasing wound redness or drainage, foul-smelling discharge, worsening pain, persistent vomiting, a catheter that stops draining or new difficulty passing urine. A painful swollen leg needs urgent same-day assessment. Complete inability to urinate needs immediate emergency assessment. Do not wait for a scheduled follow-up.

Get emergency help immediately for chest pain or breathlessness, coughing blood, fainting or loss of consciousness, heavy bleeding with dizziness or fainting, or sudden severe abdominal pain. These can indicate a clot, significant bleeding or another serious complication. Mild discharge can occur during healing, but increasing or troublesome bleeding should be reported rather than normalized by its colour or duration.

Follow-up and the longer-term outlook

Follow-up checks cancer control, healing, bladder and bowel function, lymph swelling, sexual wellbeing and pregnancy plans. The team sets examination, HPV testing and any imaging according to treatment and risk; ordinary screening schedules do not replace cancer follow-up. Report new or persistent symptoms between appointments.

Ask for a written summary of the operation, pathology, stitch and ongoing plan. Trachelectomy can offer selected people meaningful pregnancy options, but additional treatment may change them. Decisions should protect cancer care while respecting your goals, with continuing support whether pregnancy happens or not.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NCI stage-based guidance and specialist ESGO recommendations support carefully selected fertility-sparing treatment, with cancer type, margins and nodes central to decisions.

Current NHS specialist patient information describes variable recovery and bladder support; local timings differ and must not become universal rules.

CDC information distinguishes common HPV from cancer and bases cervical screening on anatomy and individual risk.

Pregnancy after trachelectomy requires specialist care; fertility preservation and a permanent stitch do not guarantee a live birth.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to keep your operation summary, pathology questions, medicines, catheter plan, symptoms and appointments together. Notes cannot assess cancer margins, rule out recurrence or a postoperative emergency, or clear you for sex or pregnancy.

When to seek help

Follow your surgical team's plan. Get emergency help for chest pain, breathlessness, coughing blood, fainting or loss of consciousness, heavy bleeding with faintness, sudden severe abdominal pain or complete inability to urinate. Fever, foul discharge, worsening wounds, a blocked catheter or a painful swollen leg need urgent assessment. Do not delay care to record symptoms.

Evidence notes updated: October 11, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Simple and radical trachelectomy remove different amounts of tissue while retaining the womb.
  • Eligibility depends on full cancer assessment, not tumour size or a positive HPV result alone.
  • Keeping the womb may preserve pregnancy options but cannot guarantee fertility or cancer outcome.
  • Recovery, catheter use, sex, work and trying for pregnancy need individual clearance.
  • Heavy bleeding with faintness, chest or breathing symptoms, fainting or loss of consciousness or inability to urinate need emergency care.

Frequently asked questions

Why is the cervix removed?

Selected early cervical cancer may be treated with trachelectomy while retaining the womb. A positive HPV test alone does not justify it. The specialist team determines the least extensive safe treatment.

Is every trachelectomy radical?

No. Simple surgery removes less surrounding tissue. A cone biopsy may suffice for some very early cancers; other findings need radical surgery or a different treatment. Ask which operation and node assessment are planned.

What is the main benefit compared with hysterectomy?

The womb remains, so carrying a pregnancy may still be possible. This is not a guarantee of conception, a live birth or equivalent outcomes for every cancer.

What are the main disadvantages?

Bleeding, infection, clots, organ or nerve injury, bladder problems, lymph swelling, painful periods or sex and fertility or pregnancy difficulties are possible. Individual risks depend on the procedure and other treatment.

How long does recovery take?

Usually several weeks, sometimes longer. Hospital stay, catheter removal and return to driving, work or sex vary; follow your team's instructions rather than a universal three-to-five-day admission or four-to-six-week deadline.

Can I become pregnant afterwards?

Some people can, naturally or with fertility treatment. Obtain cancer-team clearance and specialist pregnancy care. Miscarriage and premature birth risks are increased; a permanent cerclage requires caesarean delivery.

Do I still need follow-up after the cervix is removed?

Yes. Specialist cancer follow-up and any recommended HPV testing or other investigations remain important. Report new symptoms without waiting for the next appointment.

Which symptoms require immediate help?

Chest pain, breathlessness, coughing blood, fainting or loss of consciousness, heavy bleeding with faintness, sudden severe abdominal pain or complete inability to urinate require emergency assessment. Fever, foul discharge, worsening wounds or a painful swollen leg need urgent clinical advice.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
